item.title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests (198 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www1.wdr.de/nrw/rheinland/rhein-erft-kreis/technischer-defekt-chlor-phantasialand-100.html, See on Hacker News

Diesem Problem waren wir alle ausgesetzt: Am Freitag gab es eine Störung, die den US-Softwarekonzern Microsoft lahmgelegt hat. Unter anderem das E-Mail-Programm Outlook.

Betroffen war auch das Phantasialand. Durch die Störung kamen keine Mails an, wie das Unternehmen dem WDR am Samstag mitteilte. So bekam niemand mit, dass das Wartungssicherheitssystem der Saunalandschaft längst per Mail Alarm geschlagen hat. Denn das automatischen Dosiersystem hatte zu viel Chlor in den Pool gepumpt.

Reizungen der Atemwege

Dadurch wurden Gäste im Hotel Ling Bao des Phantasialands in Brühl verletzt. Sie haben über gesundheitliche Probleme geklagt, nachdem sie den Pool besucht hatten. Der wurde zeitweise gesperrt, konnte inzwischen aber wieder freigegeben werden, wie die Feuerwehr am Samstag dem WDR mitteilte.

Wegen der Beschwerden der Hotel-Besucher wurden Rettungskräfte und die Feuerwehr gerufen. 13 Gäste klagten über Reizungen der Atemwege, letztlich stieg die Zahl der Betroffenen auf insgesamt 15.

Zunächst hieß es, dass fünf Gäste ins Krankenhaus gebracht wurden, später wurde die Zahl auf vier korrigiert, eine Person davon blieb wegen einer mittelschweren Verletzung zur Beobachtung im Krankenhaus.

Überhöhter Chlorgehalt

Im Hotel ergaben Tests der Einsatzkräfte einen Defekt des automatischen Dosiersystems für den Pool. Dies hatte zu einem deutlich überhöhten Chlorgehalt geführt. Das Wasser wurde daher ausgetauscht.

'Duffy Lied': Controllers Refute Transportation Secretary's Ground Stop Story (121 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.commondreams.org/news/duffy-ground-stop-explanation, See on Hacker News

Air traffic controllers are rejecting US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's explanation for Friday's nationwide flight ground stop, raising questions about the Trump administration's account of a communications failure that disrupted air travel across the United States, affecting an estimated 1.5 million travelers.

Washington Examiner homeland security reporter Anna Giaritelli told CNN's Laura Coates during a Friday night interview that she'd spoken with 60 air traffic controllers about the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop, which was just the third to ever occur.

"None of them are buying what he said," Giaritelli said. "The controllers were saying, 'We don’t buy that this is actually what’s happening, the reason that Sean Duffy is saying this has happened.'"

At a White House briefing Friday evening, Duffy blamed the disruption on America's aging air traffic control infrastructure, saying overloaded switches and routers had produced inconsistent radar and communications data.

“Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data,” he said. “And because of that, we shut the system down.”

But Giaritelli said the controllers she contacted questioned the plausibility of the administration's account, particularly the timing of the alleged equipment changes.

“These types of switches... that the FAA is doing, they don't happen during the day,” she told Coates. “They don't happen during busy times like a Friday afternoon. They're doing these midweek, middle of the night, when there is no air traffic going on."

Giaritelli's comments came as the Trump administration struggled to explain how a failure in the nation's air traffic control network could have escalated into a shutdown affecting airports nationwide. The FAA lifted the ground stop at approximately 8:15 pm Eastern on Friday, but the disruption continued Saturday.

Duffy offered a new detail on Saturday, saying that a system overload occurred when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing a section of the air traffic control system’s old copper wire with new fiber wire.

“Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment,” the secretary said, adding that officials were investigating whether the contractor's "incompetence" or a faulty router was to blame.

Duffy emphatically denied that the FAA's recent nationwide rollout of an $875 million artificial intelligence system called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories (SMART) had anything to do with Friday's disruption, claiming that the system "is not even plugged in."

The FAA said earlier this week that it "will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 [air traffic control] centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption, and improve the travel experience for the flying public."

Duffy also used the crisis to renew his demand for $50 billion in congressional funding to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system, arguing that the aging infrastructure would continue to fail without additional investment.

The administration's shifting account has added to calls for an independent investigation. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday that investigators had found no evidence of a cyberattack, although he acknowledged that the possibility had not been entirely ruled out.

Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) was among those who challenged the administration's explanation, suggesting that Duffy had concealed the role of the Trump administration's own modernization efforts.

Walkinshaw cited a September report from the Government Accountability Office warning that precisely this could happen.

“In essence, the FAA is buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions," GAO said. "The net effect could be that air traffic controllers are forced to continue to rely on severely outdated systems that are prone to failure leading to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, or worse—safety incidents.”

The fiasco prompted critics, including Democratic New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, to call for Duffy's resignation.

"From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy’s watch," Hochul wrote on Facebook.

"Through it all, he’s been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency," she added, referring to the former MTV "Real World: Boston" and "Road Rules: All Stars" participant's "The Great American Road Trip" travel series, which features his family, including his wife, Fox News personality Rachel Campos Duffy.

The ground stop was the longest nationwide aviation shutdown in 25 years, with more than 3,500 aircraft already airborne when the FAA ordered the grounding. More than 4,100 flights were canceled Saturday alone, according to FlightAware.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that normal operations were expected to resume by Sunday evening.

item.title: Emacs Is My Browser (143 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://joshblais.com/blog/emacs-as-my-browser/, See on Hacker News

In my ever-increasing desire to use emacs as my sole computing environment, I have started to take browsing the web inside it far more seriously. Where I previously had thought EWW to be a niceity but far from capable, after using it for a few days it seems to be useable for about 85-90% of use cases - even on the javascript riddled hellhole that is the internet.

Why?#

I have seen in my own use of the modern browser (chromium/firefox) that it is far too easy to get distracted - too easy to get off track and fall down rabbit holes that take over my day. There are infinite suggestions as to how I should spend my time, uncountable shiny objects that take my eye off the prize that is Creativity and Depth. This has been momentously negated with EWW (or any terminal browser, lynx or browsh for the non-emacs users).

In addition to this, my belief is that we should make strides toward leaving behind Layer 8 of the internet - the limiting frontends of social platforms and locked away corners of the net that limit actual discourse (Discord, I’m looking at you). We have given up far too much to big tech platforms, and gotten nothing of value in return, to the point that many now think the internet is dying.

The internet is just a delivery mechanism, and for people that see it for what it really is, the internet has never been more alive. I truly recommend using the internet as if it was 1999.

Even on my phone, I’ve stopped using javascript frontends and embraced using eww in emacs (in termux), only falling back to fennec for about 5-10% of usecases:

I find this way of using the internet far higher in signal than any other method, allowing me to look up information, read documentation, and produce more.

How I am doing this#

For the uninitiated, emacs ships with EWW (Emacs Web Wowser) permitting you to browse the web with image and gif (when did gifs die, I almost never see them these days!) support directly inside Emacs.

I have some sane defaults that permit ease of use such as using B for back, U for yanking url at point, and a few built in functions.

Hitting R will invoke eww readable which is similar to reader mode in firefox, removing headers and footers and focusing in on the text on page. Useful.

You can send the page to your default browser with &. If a page doesn’t render nicely, this is a good fallback.

D will download images locally, b goes back a page, a will save bookmarks. All of this makes browsing in eww truly enjoyable.

I have also set .pdf to open in emacs, .mp4 and youtube/video hosting links to open in mpv, and gopher/gemini links to open in elpher. Elpher is the EWW for the gopher and gemini protocols, the smolweb that is all signal and no noise.

EWW uses Shr to render html, so you will see some callouts to that in my configuration below:

My browser.el setup:#

Here’s how I have configured EWW to work in my Emacs configuration:

My default search engine is my own Searx instance, a privacy respecting frontend that amalgamates all other search engines.

Limitations#

You will not be watching youtube videos or reading Tweets (x.com is adversarial to non-JS supported browsers). You will not be using social media, nor will you be logging into any platforms. You will not be doing your online banking, filling in government forms, or viewing client portals.

The usecase is quick web searches, documentation, and reading blogs generally. Once more, hitting & in any web page will bring up your default browser to continue your session in chromium or firefox when you do run into pages that don’t work well in EWW.

Conclusion#

I have reverted all my url functions to default to browsing in EWW, so any web interaction must first go through EWW. This has encouraged me to deeply consider what I am doing online first and foremost, and then only falling back to a modern browser when needed. I have been pleasantly surprised with how much I am able to do inside emacs, and continue to move toward using it as my computing environment in perpetuity.

As always, God bless, and until next time.

If you enjoyed this post, consider Supporting my work, Checking out my book, Working with me, or sending me an Email to tell me what you think.

item.title: All AI-generated code should be Open Source (951 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://jakub.jankiewicz.org/blog/ai-code-open-source/, See on Hacker News

This may be a hot take, but I strongly believe that all code generated by AI should be Open Source. And here's why.

First of all, AI models were trained on a massive corpus of Open Source code written since RMS announced the GNU Project and the Free Software Movement. That code was simply scraped from the internet and used without permission or proper attribution. The models were also trained on Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange sister projects, which are released under Creative Commons licenses that legally require attribution. Turning this collective knowledge into proprietary, closed-source code feels like license laundering.

The second reason is legal: purely AI-generated code is not written by a human, meaning it should not be copyrightable. The foundation for this principle in the US goes back to the famous Monkey Selfie dispute, which established that non-humans cannot hold copyrights. A precedent later cited by the U.S. Copyright Office regarding AI. Following the same logic, Wikimedia Commons requires all purely AI-generated images to be tagged as Public Domain.

However, copyright laws differ across the globe. For instance, countries like the UK grant limited copyright protection to computer-generated works. To make things fair across all jurisdictions, and to honor the open ecosystem that made AI possible, developers and companies should explicitly release AI-generated code under Open Source licenses or dedicate it to the public domain using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) license.

Of course, code is not always 100% manual or 100% automated. However, developers more and more rely on AI without even reviewing the generated output, let alone modifying it to fit their specific needs. Code like this, where humans put little effort, except writing prompts, should definitely be Open Source.

If you find this article interesting you may want to follow me on Twitter: @jcubic and on LinkedIn.

item.title: Things That Turbo Pascal Is Smaller Than (2011) (163 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://prog21.dadgum.com/116.html, See on Hacker News

Turbo Pascal 3 for MS-DOS was released in September 1986. Being version 3, there were lesser releases prior to it and flashier ones after, but 3 was a solid representation of the Turbo Pascal experience: a full Pascal compiler, including extensions that it made it practical for commercial use, tightly integrated with an editor. And the whole thing was lightning fast, orders of magnitude faster at building projects than Microsoft's compilers.

The entire Turbo Pascal 3.02 executable--the compiler and IDE--was 39,731 bytes. How does that stack up in 2011 terms? Here are some things that Turbo Pascal is smaller than, as of October 30, 2011:

The minified version of jquery 1.6 (90,518 bytes).

The yahoo.com home page (219,583 bytes).

The image of the white iPhone 4S at apple.com (190,157 bytes).

zlib.h in the Mac OS X Lion SDK (80,504 bytes).

The touch command under OS X Lion (44,016 bytes).

Various vim quick reference cards as PDFs. (This one is 47,508 bytes.)

The compiled code for the Erlang R14B02 parser (erl_parse.beam, 286,324 bytes).

The Wikipedia page for C++ (214,251 bytes).

(If you liked this, you might like A Personal History of Compilation Speed.)

item.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs (175 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/understanding-positional-embeddings, See on Hacker News

This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.

Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.

But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.

Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover

  • different positional methods in LLMs;

  • (finally) how RoPE works;

  • what methods are used by recent open LLMs.

Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch). If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher:

The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style.

PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.

PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, Positional choices in modern architectures.

Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the web view here, which also has a navigation bar on the left side.

Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token.

The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation.

A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention.

We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed.

Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example:

  1. “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.”

  2. “The gray fox jumps over the red fox.”

Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure.

For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7.

(If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my tokenizer materials on GitHub.)

Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer.

Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair.

GPT-style models do use a causal (autoregressive) mask, which restricts each token to itself and earlier tokens. Interestingly, this causal mask gives the computation some implicit order information. In our example, “jumps” can attend to “red” in the first sentence and “gray” in the second. So, a causal LLM can theoretically already distinguish these sentences even without explicit positional embeddings. (We will return to this idea later when discussing the “NoPE” concept.)

Nonetheless, GPT-2 and most newer LLMs include explicit positional information because it gives attention a direct signal about positions. That’s because even though the causal mask determines which tokens are accessible and provides implicit order information, it doesn’t distinguish a separation of one position from a separation of ten, for example. So, explicit positional methods are still useful (or even essential), since they supply that information.

If this all sounded confusing, don’t worry, it was more meant as an overview, and we will step through these concepts a bit more slowly in the remaining article.

We briefly talked about implicit positional information through causal attention masks (and we will revisit this again in more detail later). However, we now switch gears and talk about the explicit ways to add positional information.

The perhaps simplest and most direct (but not “cheapest”) approach is to give each sequence position its own vector. We add that vector to the token embedding, so the resulting, modified embedding vector is then passed to the first transformer block. This exact procedure is discussed in the following subsections.

To illustrate the use of an explicit, learned positional vector to the input embeddings, let’s consider GPT-2 as a concrete example. GPT-2 learns a table of position vectors during training. The following figure illustrates where these vectors are used in the architecture, that is, immediately after the token embedding lookup and before the first transformer block.

The positional embedding layer depicted in the figure above follows the same implementation as the token embedding layer, i.e., they have exactly the same output dimensions so that the resulting input vectors can be added to each other. The code below shows that with an excerpt of a GPT-2 code implementation:

And in mathematical terms, we can write it as follows. Let m be a position index and xm the token ID at that position. The input to the first block is

Here,

  • Etoken is the embedding layer,

  • Pm is the position info vector selected by m,

  • and hm is the resulting summed embedding and position vector.

The two vectors have the same width, so we add their entries element-wise. Figure 6 below shows this visually with a small numerical example.

In the figure above, at position 0, adding the token embedding [1, 1, 1] to the position embedding [1.1, 1.2, 1.3] gives [2.1, 2.2, 2.3]. By the way, the values in the figure are chosen to keep the illustration simple; in a real example, both embedding layers (tables) are initialized with small random values and learned during training.

So, what we covered in this section is a so-called absolute positional method because the positional embedding Pm depends on the token’s own position m. In the previous example sentence, the two “fox” tokens have initially the same token embeddings, but because we are adding different positional vectors P2 and P7, they have different values before they enter the first transformer block. And consequently, the query, key, and value vectors inside the attention mechanisms then also receive representations that already include position information.

Note that the original GPT-2 implementation has 1,024 learned position vectors. This means it only works with inputs with 1024 or fewer tokens. If we want to extend the context window, we would have to extend this embedding table. And since the embedding table (layer) is updated like any other layer during training, the context length would have to be decided before the training starts.

Extending the context would be very expensive since the table can become very large. For example, in the case of GPT-2 Medium, the positional embedding layer weights only make up 0.30% of the total weights at 1,024 positions. However, if we increased the context length to a nowadays common 100k range, they would make up >22% of the total model weights, which would be very uneconomic.

The original “Attention Is All You Need” transformer from 2017, which predates GPT, uses the same addition mechanism, but computes its position vectors with fixed sine and cosine functions. Figure 7 below shows this addition before both the encoder and decoder stacks. The encoder processes the input sequence, and the decoder generates the output sequence. (The reason why it’s introduced here is that the sine and cosine functions will become relevant again later when discussing RoPE.)

The original transformer also scales its token embeddings by √(dmodel) before adding the position vectors, where dmodel is the embedding width.

So, while GPT-2 in the previous section had the formula

the formula used in the original transformer (depicted in Figure 7) is:

This scaling by √(dmodel) is a minor technical detail, but for those who are curious, the motivation behind this scaling factor is not explained in the transformer paper, but as I discussed with colleagues on a Twitter thread many years ago, it’s likely to put the token embeddings and sinusoidal positional encodings on comparable numerical scales at initialization, so the position vectors don’t dominate the sum when we add them.

In the GPT-2 case, this scaling wasn’t necessary because the original GPT-2 code initialized the token embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.02 and the position embeddings to have an initial standard deviation of 0.01 so that they were already roughly on the same scale.

Now, the more interesting point is how the position embeddings Pm are computed.

Concretely, each position vector has the following entries:

As before, m denotes the position. The index i indexes a pair of features within the vector.

Here, a feature is one number in the position vector. For example, let’s assume we have a small vector with 8 values (dmodel = 8) that has entries numbered 0 through 7. (In the original paper this was 512 for the small model and 1024 for the bigger model, instead of 8, but that would be hard to visualize.) We group these into four pairs so that i goes from 0 through 3.

Here, the indices 2i and 2i + 1 select the two entries corresponding to pair i.

As shown in the equation earlier, the angle at position m, which is then fed into the sine or cosine functions to obtain Pm, 2i or Pm, 2i + 1, respectively, is computed as follows:

Figure 10 shows this calculation for all four pairs of our 8-feature example at position m = 2.

For an eight-feature embedding, the four frequencies are 1, 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001 radians per position. At position 2, the first pair in row 1 is (sin 2, cos 2) ≈ (0.909, −0.416).

The second pair, in row 2, changes more slowly, giving (sin 0.2, cos 0.2) ≈ (0.199, 0.980).

The figure below visualizes the sine and cosine calculations for different pairs, which are then collected in a position vector.

In short, this method is a (more complicated) alternative to obtaining positional embedding vectors compared to the GPT-2 method discussed earlier.

Similar to the GPT-2 embeddings, these are also absolute embeddings because each vector is computed from its own position. However, in contrast to the GPT-2 approach, the sine and cosine functions stay fixed during training. (Also, they can be extended and evaluated beyond the training positions, like beyond the context length of 1024, although that alone doesn’t guarantee that the model will perform well there, because it hasn’t seen those during training.)

To summarize, Figure 12 below compares the two ways of obtaining a position vector we discussed so far.

This sinusoidal method may look like an overly complicated way to obtain positional embeddings, however, understanding it will be useful when talking about RoPE in the next section.

Also, there is some rationale behind it. The authors chose sine and cosine because they make the shifting by a certain offset gives a certain deterministic difference. For example, the difference between position 2 to 5 and the difference between 102 to 105 is both 3, which then results in the same rotation.

According to the Attention Is All You Need paper:

“...easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PEpos + k can be represented as a linear function of PEpos.”

Or in less technical terms, the authors hypothesized that this property would make it easier for attention to learn relationships such as “three tokens earlier.”

Figure 13 below illustrates this for one sine/cosine pair. A rotation is a linear transformation, and both three-position shifts use the same rotation.

So, the sinusoidal method above is still considered an absolute positional encoding because the vector added to each token embedding represents that token’s position counted from the start of the sequence.

As shown in the previous figure, for example, tokens at positions 2 and 5 receive the position vectors P2 and P5. If we move those tokens to positions 102 and 105, they’re still three positions apart. But each token gets a different position vector because its absolute position m has changed.

So their attention score can change even when the token embeddings stay the same. The sinusoidal structure still gives the model a way to learn relative relationships.

Anyways, RoPE, which we will discuss below, builds this relative relationship directly into the attention calculation. RoPE, which Su et al. introduced in the 2021 RoFormer paper, stands for Rotary Position Embedding and is considered a relative position method.

In attention, each token’s current representation is projected into a query, a key, and a value vector. Query-key dot products determine attention scores. After masking and softmax, the resulting weights determine how the value vectors are mixed. For a refresher, see my Understanding and Coding Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention, Causal-Attention, and Cross-Attention in LLMs article:

RoPE uses the token’s position to rotate its query and key vectors before their dot product. The value vectors bypass this rotation. Figure 14 below shows an overview of where RoPE is applied in a relatively recent MiniMax-M3, where QK-Norm normalizes queries and keys before RoPE.

As shown in the figure above, the LLM architecture has no explicit position vector added alongside the initial token embedding. Its explicit position signal is injected inside attention instead.

Side note: MiniMax-M3 rotates only part of each query and key head, a variation known as “partial RoPE” that we will cover later in Section 6.1. But to understand the basic RoPE operation first, let’s walk through the method step by step using a small example.

Attention usually divides its query, key, and value features into multiple heads, which are processed in parallel. Hence, the full mechanism is usually called Multi-head Attention (note that Grouped Query Attention also uses multiple heads). Here, each attention head computes its own attention scores and weighted sums. RoPE then acts on pairs of numbers within each query and key head.

To make this concrete, Figure 12 below follows a token representation through the learned query and key projections, which are computed via the weight matrices WQ and WK. In this toy example, each projection produces 16 features, which are reshaped into two heads with eight features each. In the figure below, every small cell contains one scalar feature, meaning one numerical entry in a vector (the numbers are not shown due to space reasons).

For the first eight-feature head, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], we pair each feature in the first half with the corresponding feature in the second half. This gives (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7), and (4, 8). This split-half convention is used in LLM implementations, including my Qwen3 implementation. (We will compare it with the original, alternative adjacent-feature pairing method later after implementing the basic operation.)

Each pair gets a rotation angle determined by the token position m and that pair’s frequency θi. The corresponding query and key pairs use the same frequency. Figure 16 below shows how we rotate the pairs, put the updated features back in their original locations, and compute the query-key dot product.

The next section will walk through the figure(s) a bit more slowly.

For the following example, we’ll use the same two positions as before. The query comes from “the” at position m = 5, and the key comes from the first “fox” at position n = 2. Since, in this example, the key comes before the query, the causal mask allows the query to attend to it.

To illustrate the effect that the position has, and keeping everything fixed, let’s assume we start both pairs from the same two values, (1, 5).

Furthermore, for this example, let’s use θ = 20° per token position (π/9 radians per position). At position 2, we rotate the key’s arrow counterclockwise by 2 × 20° = 40°. At position 5, we rotate the query’s arrow by 5 × 20° = 100°.

To illustrate what’s happening in the figure above, for example, plugging cos 40° ≈ 0.766 and sin 40° ≈ 0.643 into the rotation from Figure 16 gives the new key coordinates:

Then, changing 40° to 100°, using the same equation as above, the rotated query pair becomes q′ ≈ (−5.098, 0.117). But the important point is that both arrows still have length √26. Only the rotation changes but the vectors keep the same lengths after the transformation.

So, for a query pair (a, b) at position m, the two operations here are.

For the key pair at position n, we use the same equations with nθ.

(Section 4 later shows how RoPE calculates the angular frequency for each feature pair.)

To close this section, for those more comfortable reading code, everything about RoPE illustrated so far can be written in code, as follows:

The resulting values are:

Original key:   (1, 5)
Original query: (1, 5)
Rotated key:    (-2.448, 4.473)
Rotated query:  (-5.098, 0.117)

If we rotate all 4 pairs in the 8-feature query (and key) vector(s), we get the vectors below. (We’ll come back to how we go from rotating one pair to rotating all of them later.)

Original key:   (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8)
Original query: (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8)
Rotated key:    (-2.448, 1.577, 2.951, 3.994, 4.473, 6.125, 7.021, 8.003)
Rotated query:  (-5.098, 0.928, 2.877, 3.986, 0.117, 6.256, 7.051, 8.007)

Note that, as shown above, the query and key heads have eight features each, which we previously grouped into 4 pairs with two elements each, like (1, 5), and (2, 6), and so on. For simplicity here we’ll follow just the first pair in each head, (1, 5), formed by taking the entries at indices 0 and 4:

Original key:   (1, 5)
Original query: (1, 5)
Rotated key:    (-2.448, 4.473)
Rotated query:  (-5.098, 0.117)

As shown above, in our example, those entries have values (1, 5) in both heads before the rotation.

Also, as in the code above, let’s use the notation q =(q1, q2) and k =(k1, k2) for these two pairs. To compute their dot product, using the standard dot product formula, we multiply corresponding coordinates and add the products:

Before rotation, the pairs have a dot product of 1 × 1 + 5 × 5 = 26. Using the rounded coordinates from the previous Figure 18 gives the contribution from the first pair after rotation:

We can see why by writing the dot product in terms of the lengths of the two vectors (arrows in Figure 18) and the angle ϕ between them.

In both cases, the vector length is √26. The query (position 5) is rotated by 100° and the key (position 2) is rotated by 40°. The vectors (arrows) start from the same direction, so they end up being 60° apart after rotation. Their exact dot product is 26 × cos(60°) = 13.

Now let’s see what happens if we move just the key from position 2 to position 3, but we keep its starting coordinates (1, 5) fixed. The key’s rotation changes now from 2 × 20° = 40° to 3 × 20° = 60°. The query still rotates by 100°, so the angle between the arrows shrinks to 40° and the dot product changes from 13 to 26 × cos(40°) ≈ 19.92. So, moving the key one position closer changed the dot product even though we started with the same feature values.

Why do these dot products matter? In attention, we sum the contributions from all feature pairs to get the query-key dot products. RoPE can change those dot products and thus the weights that softmax assigns to the value vectors.

In the attention equation above, Q′ and K′ are matrices that contain the rotated queries q′ and keys k′ for one head, V contains the values, and d is the head dimension.

Now that we illustrated the computation of the dot products, which is at the core of the attention mechanism, let’s return to positions m = 5 and n = 2. If we shift both positions to the right by three positions, we get m = 8 and n = 5. Each rotation gains 60° (the query goes from 100° to 160°, and the key goes from 40° to 100°), however, the angle between the vectors stays the same. The dot product for this feature pair is still 13.

The key is that the difference between the rotation angles is

If we keep the original query and key vectors fixed and shift both token positions by the same amount, RoPE adds the same rotation to both vectors. The angle between them stays the same, so their dot product stays the same. Note that Figure 20 below uses smaller angles than the actual example (20° per position) to keep the picture readable.

The examples above and Figure 20 illustrate the main idea behind RoPE. We use each token’s position to rotate the corresponding query and key in the attention module. In the query-key dot product, what matters is how much one vector rotates relative to the other. For each feature pair, this difference in rotation depends only on the offset between the two tokens.

To illustrate this in the big picture context, in Figure 21, each row collects the scores for one query. If we consider row 5, the query for “the”, and column 2, the key for “fox”, the attention score between those two is computed as the dot product between the two rotated versions of the query and key vector.

What’s the point, again? Let’s once more consider “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.” If we add 100 tokens (e.g., think system prompt) before the sentence, the first “fox” and the second “the” move from positions 2 and 5 to 102 and 105. However, a prefix of any length shifts both positions equally, so they still stay exactly three positions apart. This means, each vector (arrow) gains the exact same additional rotation, which preserves the angle between them and their dot product (assuming we hold the unrotated query and key vectors fixed; in a real model, a new prefix of 100 tokens can change those vectors by changing what the tokens attend to).

Figure 22 tracks this comparison in the attention score matrix. The right panel shows the rows and columns for the sentence after we add the prefix. In our toy example, the first pair still contributes 13 to the dot product.

As you may recall, in the original transformer’s sinusoidal encoding, a fixed offset also corresponds to a fixed rotation within each sine/cosine pair. But that shared rotation applies only to the position vectors (added to the input vector) instead of the key and query vectors inside the attention mechanism.

Figure 23 compares what this shift changes in the three methods we covered so far.

To see how the relative offset affects the dot product, we focused on one feature pair in the query and key. Now let’s put all four pairs together and see how RoPE rotates the full eight-feature vectors in one attention head. (Please feel free to skip this section if it is too much technical detail.)

Figure 24 picks up where Figure 17 left off. We rotate each of the four pairs, then put the results back in the query’s original feature order.

Figure 24 above shows the rotated query q′ (at the bottom). Similarly, we could get the rotated key k′ by repeating the same steps at the key’s position.

Recall the two equations from Section 3.3. For query pair i with input values (ai, bi), let ci = cos(mθi) and si = sin(mθi). These are the cosine and sine of the rotation angle for that pair at query position m:

Figure 25 below shows the same four rotations between the four pairs as a single matrix multiplication, q′ = Rmq.

A full attention head uses multiple frequencies so that some feature pairs change more drastically (”quickly” in RoPE terms) with position and others change more gradually (”slowly” in RoPE terms). This serves the same purpose as the multiple frequencies in the original transformer’s sinusoidal encodings.

However, instead of us assigning these manually, for a head with d features, standard full RoPE computes one frequency for each of its d/2 pairs as follows:

Here,

  • d is the head dimension (it has to be even so that all features can be arranged in pairs).

  • i is the index of the pair; it ranges from 0 to d/2−1.

  • b is a chosen base value (hyperparameter) that determines the spacing of the frequencies.

  • θi is pair i‘s frequency in radians per token position.

The original RoFormer paper uses b = 10,000, borrowing the original transformer’s frequency formula with head dimension d in place of embedding width dmodel.

For example, with head dimension d = 8 and base b = 10,000, we get frequencies [1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001] radians per position.

If you want to see RoPE in a complete model, I recommend checking out my end-to-end Qwen3 from-scratch implementation.

Since code can be an effective medium for explaining and understanding concepts, the following subsection will walk you through the core parts that we have covered so far, if you are interested. Otherwise, please feel free to fast forward to section 6, on Positional choices in modern architectures.

So, for the following code snippets, we’ll use the same split-half rotation convention as mentioned earlier (the interleaved convention will also be covered, no worries). First, we’ll apply it to one query vector, then we’ll use it on queries and keys inside the attention mechanism.

First, let’s reuse the 8-feature query from Figure 24. For convenience, below are its four feature pairs before rotation.

In the earlier non-coding example, we chose a frequency of 20° per token position for the first pair to keep the math simple. Here, we’ll use the original RoPE formula from the previous Section 4 above, θi = b−2i/d, with head dimension d = 8 and base b = 10,000.

Figure 26 shows how the two functions work together to apply these rotations.

As shown in the figure above, first, rope_params determines how far to rotate each pair, returning two “tables” that store the cosine and sine of those angles. Or, in other words, rope_params computes the cosine and sine of each rotation angle, which depends on the token’s position and the feature pair’s frequency.

The indices array in the rope_params function contains the 2i values from the frequency formula in Section 4:

For our eight-feature query, the indicesare [0, 2, 4, 6], that is, one 2i value for each feature pair. Suppose we use the common base b = 10,000. And following our earlier examples, we choose a small head dimension of d = 8. In this case, the inv_freq then computes the four pair frequencies θi = b−2i/d as follows:

As we can see above, the resulting inv_freq has one frequency θi for each of the four feature pairs ( measured in radians) per token position.

Next, the angles then multiplies each pair’s frequency θi with the token position m, which computes the rotation angle mθi. In our example, with positions = [2], we get:

Finally, rope_params takes the cosine and sine of each angle and outputs them as two so-called cosine and sine tables, cos and sin. In both tables, each row is a token position and each column is a feature pair. Since we only use token position 2 here, each table has shape (1, 4), with the single row shown below:

For the example in Figure 26, each table has one row for token position 2 and four columns, one for each feature pair. Figure 27 shows the rotation angle for each pair and the corresponding entries in the two tables.

In short, rope_params computes the cosine and sine of each rotation angle, which depends on the token’s position and the feature pair’s frequency.

In a real-world scenario, if we pass rope_params 1,024 token positions for a context size of 1024, and a head dimension of 128, it returns two tensors, cos and sin, each with shape (1024, 64) since a head with 128 features has 64 pairs.

The tables have no batch or head dimension, and we broadcast each (1024, 64) table across the batch and head dimensions. So, if we have multi-head attention or grouped query attention with 32 heads, feature pair 0 at token position 2 uses the same rotation angle in all 32 heads. Each head rotates its own feature values, so the rotated queries can still differ across heads. Also, the same entries can be reused across queries, keys, and heads that use the same positions and frequencies. In short, we only need to (pre)compute these tables once per model for all positions up to a maximum supported context size.

Technically, it would also be possible to store these tables alongside the model weights; but they are so incredibly cheap to compute that storing them on disk would be overkill.

Next, rope_split_half uses those cosines and sines to rotate the actual features in the query and key vectors inside attention.

Considering the simple 8-feature example once more, the .chunk in the code snippet above splits the query into [1, 2, 3, 4] and [5, 6, 7, 8] and lines up the two entries in each pair. For example, the first slot of each half gives us (1, 5), the second (2, 6), and so on. The two expressions inside torch.cat compute the rotated halves using the equations from Section 3.3:

Note that here, everything denoted with ai corresponds to the first half of the query, and everything denoted with bi comes from the second half. The first expression inside torch.cat computes all the ai′values, and the second computes all the bi′ values.

Then, we concatenate the halves, which puts each value back in its original index position via torch.cat.

Here’s the code that produces the rotated query in the earlier Figure 26. The shown reshape (1, 1, 1, 8) just brings the simple toy array into the expected format: one batch item, one head, one token, and eight features.

With several positions, each token simply picks up its own row from the cos and sin tables. Through broadcasting, PyTorch reuses these same tables across all batch items and attention heads.

So far, we coded the RoPE utility functions. Let’s now use it in the real context, the attention mechanism. Here, we use the standard frequency schedule for two 8-feature heads and four token positions. We use random query, key, and value tensors to keep the example self-contained, but as mentioned before, you can optionally also check the end-to-end Qwen3 from-scratch implementation with real query, key, and values produced by the pre-trained model.

Note that only q and k but not v pass through RoPE. The resulting raw attention scores are stored in a tensor of shape (1, 2, 4, 4), that is, one row for each query position, and a column for each key position, and 4x4 since we have four tokens where each attends to each other.

Then, using a conventional attention code implementation, the causal mask replaces the scores for future keys with negative infinity, so they get zeroed after the softmax. The resulting context tensor has shape (1, 2, 4, 8); the 4 because we have four tokens, and the 8 because the embedding dimension was originally 8.

We can also check that our claim about relative offsets holds, meaning that adding 3 to each position should change the position but preserve the query-key offsets:

I mentioned the split-halves convention many times throughout this article. The original RoPE paper uses the alternative interleaved convention, as does the original LLaMA implementation (but as mentioned before, most code implementations now use the split-halves, because it makes it easier, in code, to rotate all pairs at once with element-wise sine and cosine operations.)

To illustrate the difference between the two layouts, Figure 28 below uses the same 8-feature vector in both rows.

The interleaved implementation uses the same two equations, but selects alternating features and interleaves the outputs.

But mathematically, the layouts are equivalent when we account for the feature order. So, rearranging the entries [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] to [1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8] makes the split-half pairs adjacent with pairs (1, 5), (2, 6), and so on. If we apply the same rearrangement to both queries and keys, it results in identical dot products.

The outputs retain the reordered features, so we compare them with the split-half outputs in that same order. Applying the two layouts to the original vector however would give different scores.

RoPE has been a staple in most (open-weight) LLMs since the original LLaMA model. Of course, proprietary models may use it as well, but it’s always hard to say anything with 100% certainty about proprietary models.

However, in recent years, many architectures have been moving away from full-blown RoPE in every transformer block. In the following subsection, we will discuss some of these variants.

For instance the full RoPE implementation we discussed and implemented in the sections above rotates every feature pair in every query and key head.

In the following examples in the subsections above below, we will see that models only rotate some features within a head, other models skip RoPE in some transformer blocks, and some models use a different approach and add position information directly to their attention scores.

As discussed throughout the article, regular “full” RoPE rotates all dimensions in each query and key head. Partial RoPE is a variant that rotates only a subset, while leaving the remaining dimensions unchanged.

For example, MiniMax-M3’s configuration uses 64 rotary dimensions within each 128-dimensional head. That gives 32 rotated feature pairs and 64 unchanged dimensions. The figure below illustrates how that looks like.

Note that if we look past the first transformer block, the unrotated features can still contain position information inherited from earlier transformer blocks.

Anyways, what’s the point behind partial RoPE? It saves some memory. For example, in the MiniMax-M3 example above, rotating half the features reduces the size of the precomputed cosine and sine tables also in half. So, with partial RoPE, instead of 64 columns, now each table only needs 32 columns. However, note that the KV cache still stores the full key and value vectors for each cached token.

For MiniMax-M3’s 1M-token context, rotating 64 of the 128 features halves the size of the precomputed cosine and sine tables, saving 0.134 GB (128 MiB) if the tables are stored in BF16. If the tables themselves were stored in NVFP4, the savings would be 0.038 GB (36 MiB), including the block scales.

Note that in experiments with 1B to 8B models, the Fractional Rotation, Full Potential? paper found that rotating around 10% of each head’s features often gave similar training loss and benchmark accuracy to full RoPE. However, full RoPE did better on some evaluations.

So, in my opinion, partial RoPE is hardly worth it.

NoPE was coined in the The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers paper and means no explicit positional encoding. The idea or observation is that an attention layer without any explicit position method still has a causal mask, where a query can attend only to itself and earlier tokens. And this causal masking implicitly provides positional information.

Let’s use the first four tokens from our earlier example, The red fox jumps. In Figure 30, the query for fox at position 2 can attend to The, red, and itself. The query for red at position 1 can attend to The and itself.

So, the next question is how can the model use the causal mask as a position signal? Here’s a toy example adapted from the paper.

Suppose one feature of the value vectors is 1 for The and 0 for the other three tokens. Since the input only contains only one The, every visible prefix contains exactly one 1. If all non-masked keys get the same attention score, the softmax assigns every visible token equal weight.

So at fox, attention averages 1, 0, and 0, which gives 1/3. At jumps, it averages four values and gets 1/4. In other words, this output feature equals one over the prefix length, which a later layer can use as a signal for position.

Does NoPE work in practice? The researchers of the NoPE paper trained a tiny 107M-parameter decoder-only transformers from scratch on tasks such as copying, sorting, and addition to do some ablation.

When they tested the small model on examples longer than those seen during training, interestingly, NoPE ranked first overall across the ten tasks and ahead of RoPE. The researchers behind the NoPE paper also conducted a separate experiment with a larger 1.3B-parameter models trained on code. Here, NoPE also handled contexts beyond the training length, however, its next-token predictions got worse at the longest lengths tested.

Some of today’s open-weight LLMs even go so far and use NoPE in all layers. However, nowadays, it’s more common for models to omit RoPE in at least some layers, where layer here means transformer block.

To give a concrete example, SmolLM3 (3B parameters) applies RoPE in three layers and skips it in the fourth, repeating that pattern through 36 layers. Interestingly, the SmolLM3 authors mentioned that this layer pattern improved long-context performance.

(Also note that any later layer, following the first one, even though it may skip the rotation, still receives the inputs from preceding transformer blocks, so its queries and keys still receive some sort of position information from earlier layers.)

Before we get to the overview and look at what modern architectures use, there’s one more method to introduce. For instance, Thinky’s Inkling uses a learned relative position bias in both its sliding-window and global attention layers. It computes the usual scaled dot product between a query and key, and then it adds a certain number to that score before the softmax in the attention score computation. That number depends on the query token’s hidden state and how many positions back the key is.

Let’s reuse our example sentence, “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.” (It’s the last time, I promise!) In the figure below, the “the” at position 5 is the query and “fox” at position 2 is the key. Inkling then uses the three-position gap between query and key and the hidden state for “the” to compute the bias, then adds it to the scaled dot product.

This is not an entirely new idea. Some of you may recall Google’s popular T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) in 2019, which used a simpler version of this idea.

Now, after all this build up, the interesting question is: which architecture uses which method? And what are the recent trends?

To answer this, I grouped the entries in my LLM Architecture Gallery by their listed release dates and compared the 2025 releases with the earlier and later releases in the 2026 snapshot. Each gallery card counts once, so multiple variants of an architecture can contribute to the results. LLM Architecture Gallery

As we can see in Figure 35 above, using RoPE in every softmax attention layer is still the most common choice. However, its use fell from 2025 to 2026, and then also in the latter half of 2026, which could be a trend.

Consequently, there is a growing number of models that mix RoPE and NoPE. The groups are still small, so it’s hard to say whether these trends will continue.

The NoPE only entries were all recurrent hybrids with softmax attention layers that use no explicit positional encoding. The “Other” category here refers to xLSTM 7B (2025) and Inkling (2026). xLSTM has no softmax attention layers. Inkling adds a learned bias to the attention scores before softmax, as we saw in Section 6.3.

Among the models that use RoPE, partial RoPE became more common from 2025 to 2026. It went from a minority of the RoPE models in 2025 to a majority in both 2026 groups, as shown in Figure 36.

If you’d like to look up an individual model from the 2026 groups, Figure 37 below shows the 2026 gallery overview with the individual architectures labeled by position type. You can also browse the gallery interactively here.

So, to recap, we discussed GPT-2 and the original transformer that add a position vector to each token embedding before the first transformer block. Then, modern LLMs switched to RoPE, which encodes relative position inside attention by rotating queries and keys. Surprisingly, RoPE remains as the most popular positional embedding method today.

Recently, however, Inkling picked up an idea from T5 to add a learned relative position bias to the attention scores before softmax. And then we also have NoPE-RoPE architectures, which omit RoPE in some layers.

It may be boring news, but as mentioned before, RoPE is still the predominant position embedding method, and I think this will carry over into 2027 for sure. Perhaps, though, we’ll see more architectures with an Inkling-like design coming up in 2027.

While this may sound “boring”, I am glad that I finally got this article on RoPE (and other position info methods) out, after so many years, so that I can add it to my collection of LLM “fundamentals” explainers.

If you are interested in the other architecture building blocks of LLMs, I still highly recommend starting with a GPT-2-style model, which will give you a solid understanding of the building blocks with the least amount of friction. And from there, you can then layer on additional methods (such as RoPE).

If you’d like to build that GPT-2-style model yourself, my first Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book walks through all the building blocks depicted in the figure below.

For the methods that branch off from the GPT-2 baseline, I’ve collected some of my relevant blog articles below, starting with a refresher on self-attention:

  • Self-attention, causal masking, and multi-head attention: Understanding and Coding Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention, Causal-Attention, and Cross-Attention in LLMs

  • Modern attention variants (GQA, MLA, sliding-window attention, sparse attention, and hybrids): A Visual Guide to Attention Variants in Modern LLMs

  • The KV cache. Understanding and Coding the KV Cache in LLMs from Scratch

  • SwiGLU feed-forward layers and normalization (LayerNorm and RMSNorm): From GPT-2 to gpt-oss: Analyzing the Architectural Advances

  • Mixture-of-experts layers and expert routing. The Big LLM Architecture Comparison

  • Residual connections and DeepSeek’s manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC): Recent Developments in LLM Architectures: KV Sharing, mHC, and Compressed Attention

  • Putting some of the pieces together in Qwen3: Understanding and Implementing Qwen3 From Scratch walks through implementing the dense and mixture-of-experts versions in PyTorch.

Thanks for reading and supporting my work!

PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.

The commerce secretary has been writing new rules that would affect Southeast Asian data centers, some of which are clients of his former firm.

Nov. 15, 2026, 5:02 a.m. ET

In Malaysia’s lush southern peninsula, a data center known as A201 is set to open next year, packed with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence servers.

The data center plans to supply this computing power to a Chinese tech giant. The setup is legal and profitable. It will also sidestep U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

The company operating the data center is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who handed off leadership of it to his sons. Mr. Lutnick is now writing the rules that would have a substantial effect on the data center’s business.

Mr. Lutnick has been seen as a force slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to data centers like A201, which sit outside China but provide A.I. computing power to Chinese firms.

The Trump administration, concerned about ceding the country’s advantage in A.I., bans the sale of cutting-edge chips to China. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia. On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centers as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban. On the other are officials, most prominently Mr. Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of U.S. companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia.

Recently, Mr. Lutnick has been advocating a less stringent version of those controls under consideration, which could cut back on Nvidia’s business by giving the U.S. government more oversight of chip sales to international data centers. It is the latest example of Mr. Lutnick’s soft touch on chip regulation, which has prompted criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration.

item.title: Book list for streetfighting computer scientists (118 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://nick-black.com/dankwiki/index.php?title=Book_list_for_streetfighting_computer_scientists, See on Hacker News

2025 edition. this is very different from most "best books for programmers" lists you'll see, with Code Complete and Clean Code and Wistful Wanking for Practical Wankers and Design Slatterns and titles like that. you'll figure all that out as you go along. these are books to read so that you can cut motherfuckers with knives. do you need to read all of these? only if you want to know the things inside, i guess.

Introductory streetfighting

  • Stepanov, From Mathematics to Generic Programming and The Elements of Programming
  • Gustedt, Modern C
  • Hanson, C Interfaces and Implementations
  • Stroustrup, The C++ Programming Language
  • Josuttis, C++ Move Semantics, because a language feature requiring 200 pages of explication is worth studying? no, because this book justifies Rust better than any text on that language.
  • Klabnik, Nichols, and Krycho, The Rust Programming Language

need you write in C or C++? not generally. but they are a lingua franca, implemented on most hardware you'll meet, and serve as the native API expression of all operating system that matter. rust is a pretty good language to write and read, and much less to talk about all the fucking time, so cut that shit out.

Brawling combat

  • Dijkstra, A Discipline of Programming. the most beautiful book, page-for-page, in all of computer science.
  • Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, especially volumes 1 and 4B, third edition
  • Warren, Hacker's Delight. make sure you get the second edition
  • Stevens and Rago, Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment, get at least the second and preferably the third edition
  • Stevens, UNIX Network Programming, second edition
  • Abelson + Sussman, Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, best cover on a CS textbook hands down, second edition
  • Varghese, Networking Algorithmics
  • McKusick, The Design and Implementation of the FreeBSD Operating System
  • Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface
  • Garcia + Widjaja, Communications Networks. do you even ARQ, bro?
  • Kleinrock, Queueing Systems, especially volume 1. this is why they made you take prob/stats.
  • Hennessy + Paterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. the older editions don't lock material away from you online, but are...older.
  • Kennedy, Optimizing Compilers for Modern Architectures. if you want to actually implement compilers make sure you get Muchnik's Advanced Compiler Design and Implmentation as well
  • CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms
  • Samet, Metric and Multidimensional Data Structures
  • McKenney, Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It? despite its preposterous title, this book is excellent, and covers things you won't find anywhere else. If Naming Books is so Hard for You, Why Didn't You Ask For Help?
  • Crochemere et al, Algorithms on Strings. just as french as it sounds, a true force de frappe
  • Culler et al, Parallel Computer Architecture
  • Ward + Halstead, Computation Structures
  • Shriver + Smith, The Anatomy of a High-Performance Microprocessor
  • Vazirani, Approximation Algorithms
  • Raghaven + Motwani, Randomized Algorithms
  • Garey and Johnson, Computers and Intractability. it's always embarrassing to realize you've promised a solution to an np-complete problem.
  • Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation. but not as embarrassing as realizing you've promised a solution to an undecidable problem. also, the pumping lemma!
  • Galub + Van Loan, Matrix Computations. this is pretty much a straight mathematics textbook, but roaming multiethnic gangs of matrices make up many streetfights.

For the advanced streetfighter

  • Ahora + Barak, Computational Complexity
  • Pierce, Types and Programming Languages
  • Okasaki, Purely Functional Data Structures
  • Van Roy + Hardidi, Concepts, Techniques, and Models of Computer Programming
  • Barendregt, The Lambda Calculus. it is true that the λ-cube is rarely useful within the tight confines of a knifefight. after a long day of bandanas and leather gloves and switchblades, even the brawler must eventually go home to family and fire and food and F systems. in a pinch, its bedazzling yellow cover can blind opponents.

speaking of math, you might want to take a look at Axler's Linear Algebra Done Right and Knuth's Concrete Mathematics. you'll want to know your combinatorics, your prob/stats, and your linear algebra cold. calculus through diffeqs is necessary to know, but i'm a pretty hardcore nerd and yet don't find myself integrating things all that often.

now go forth and fight in the streets. i list no machine learning because i dislike machine learning. there are no quantum books because quantum is not yet useful for streetfighting (we all look forward to this situation changing). i list no SIMT/accelerator books because they're all shite. i list no infosec because infosec is a subfield of QA, fight me. there are no links because i'm a lazy, lazy man.

i've heard good things about Tim Roughgarden's algorithms books, and have them on my shelves to read soon, but cannot yet speak to them. likewise Beej's book on networking, though that looks kinda lightweight. neither he nor Stevens goes into modern fast networking using things like XDP and Io_uring.

you should of course also read Hacking the Planet with Notcurses, buying copies for your team and family.

item.title: We're Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches (325 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/11/were-asking-appeals-court-require-warrant-alpr-searches, See on Hacker News

Today, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant, a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.

Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places.

But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin, ALPRs give law enforcement “a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment.

We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant.

Related Updates

We Demand More Information on How Marin Cops Illegally Shared Flock ALPR Data

The Marin County Sheriff’s Office is the latest California law enforcement agency to get caught sharing automated license plate reader (ALPR) data from their Flock Safety system with out-of-state and federal agencies. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California are calling them out for this direct violation of California law,...

The High Crime of “LMAO”: How Cops Are Treating Flock's Mass Surveillance As a Joke

With no warrant requirements, limited guardrails, and deficient audit processes, ALPR databases have fostered a culture of unrestricted access to everyone’s location information. This culture of abuse has allowed police to treat a mass surveillance network like their own personal search engine, permitting the tracking of the movements of everyday...

Texas and Florida Step Back from ALPRs

Within the last few days, two important state actions have dealt a big blow to automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks. This is just the latest proof of the growing tide of public opposition to mass surveillance. After years of successful grassroots battles to pull these cameras from local streets...

item.title: Court denies motion to dismiss DRAM price fixing case (465 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://litnews.ai/articles/garciaguirre-samsung-sk-hynix-micron-dram-conspiracy-suit-survives-dismissal, See on Hacker News

Key Points

  • Judge Noël Wise denied in full Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron's joint motion to dismiss a proposed class action alleging they conspired to cut supply of conventional DRAM, such as DDR5, and shift capacity to HBM.
  • The court held the case was not a rerun of DRAM II, the Ninth Circuit's 2022 affirmance of dismissal of an earlier DRAM conspiracy suit against the same companies.
  • The judge found that long-term HBM lock-ups, refusals of long-term conventional DRAM contracts, Micron's Crucial closure, fab delays, the failure to expand despite record prices, near-identical customer vetting and the companies' prior cartel history supported a plausible inference of conspiracy.
  • The court gave no weight to three of the plaintiffs' arguments: investor statements about "supply discipline," which it found too similar to statements the Ninth Circuit's DRAM II decision had already held insufficient; executives' meetings at industry conferences, since DRAM II all but forecloses relying on them unless plaintiffs identify what was actually exchanged or agreed there; and the three-company market structure, which it called neutral.
  • Answers are due Dec. 7, 2026, and the initial case management conference was reset for Jan. 12, 2027.

A federal judge on Nov. 14 refused to dismiss a proposed class action accusing Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron of conspiring to restrict the supply of conventional dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, the standardized memory chips used in computers, phones and servers.

U.S. District Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California denied the companies' joint motion to dismiss in full, finding the complaint plausibly alleged an agreement in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The allegations, accepted as true at this stage, have not been proven.

The companies argued the case was a rerun of DRAM II, in which the Ninth Circuit in 2022 affirmed dismissal of claims against the same three companies over a 2016–2018 supply restriction. "The Court finds that it is not," Judge Wise wrote.

The suit was filed June 25, 2026, by 17 consumers and small businesses from five states. It concerns conventional DRAM, which the complaint describes as "standardized memory built to industry specifications and sold for ordinary purposes," including DDR5 generation modules built for computers.

According to the complaint, the three companies controlled more than 91% of global DRAM revenue as of the third quarter of 2025. They allegedly cut production starting in late 2022 and, beginning in 2023, shifted capacity to high bandwidth memory, or HBM, a specialized DRAM product for artificial intelligence accelerators that "requires approximately three to four times the silicon wafer area per gigabyte compared to conventional DDR5 DRAM."

By the third quarter of 2025, conventional DRAM prices had risen 171.8% in one year, according to the complaint, which alleges a 697% increase over 18 months. Yet "not one of the three Defendants expanded or announced plans to meaningfully expand commodity DRAM production capacity," the complaint alleges.

Without direct evidence of an agreement, the plaintiffs needed plus factors, additional facts suggesting a preceding agreement rather than conscious parallelism, in which competitors independently make similar moves.

Judge Wise rejected the companies' argument that timing gaps undercut parallel action. SK Hynix and Micron announced cuts three weeks apart in late 2022, she noted, and Samsung's lag of about four and a half months, until April 7, 2023, was "not such an unreasonably long delay that it defeats an allegation of parallel conduct on a motion to dismiss."

She found the complaint plausibly alleged that the three companies acted in parallel when they cut supply, shifted production from conventional DRAM such as DDR5 to HBM, and wound down DDR4.

Under Ninth Circuit precedent, action against self-interest must be "so perilous in the absence of advance agreement that no reasonable firm would make the challenged move without such an agreement." Judge Wise wrote that a pivot to HBM by itself "might not be sufficient," but that "the related conduct tips this factor over the edge to weigh in Plaintiffs' favor."

According to the complaint, all three signed long-term contracts locking in HBM supply, Samsung and SK Hynix reportedly refused long-term agreements with major conventional DRAM customers, and Micron announced on Dec. 3, 2025, that it would close Crucial, its 30-year-old consumer brand. Those moves, which she called "difficult if not impossible to unwind," plus the failure to expand despite record prices, "are the sort that at the pleading stage, it appears no reasonable firm would make without a prior agreement," she wrote.

She applied similar reasoning to allegations that Samsung and Micron delayed or halted new DRAM plants, citing the Ninth Circuit's 1990 Petroleum Products decision that "Changes in refinery capacity are not readily reversible." "The Court views the commitment to build or not build manufacturing capacity as analogous," she wrote. She also counted the companies' alleged same-quarter 2025 decisions to wind down DDR4 as a plus factor, citing the complaint's allegation that "older, slower DDR4 came to cost more per gigabyte than newer, faster DDR5."

Judge Wise found that near-identical customer-vetting practices all three companies allegedly adopted in January 2026 "strongly support a plausible inference of conspiracy." She rejected the companies' "obvious and non-conspiratorial explanation" of booming AI demand, noting that the vetting began after the AI boom and the HBM pivot were underway.

The court gave no weight to three other arguments. Judge Wise held that investor statements, including Micron's 2022 reference to "supply discipline," did not distinguish the case from DRAM II. Though the conference-meeting allegations went beyond those in DRAM II, she wrote that DRAM II "seemingly all but forecloses a trial court from giving any weight to trade conference meetings" absent specifics, and she called the market's oligopolistic structure "neutral in the analysis."

According to the complaint, the companies and two other manufacturers formed a criminal cartel to fix DRAM prices from 1998 to 2002; Samsung paid a $300 million fine, Hynix paid $185 million, and Micron received immunity for cooperating as a whistleblower. Judge Wise, like the DRAM II court, rejected the argument that the now-20-year-old history should not count.

At the hearing, the companies quoted the late Judge Posner's line that competitors in concentrated markets "watch each other like hawks." Judge Wise wrote: "But Plaintiffs' allegations go beyond hawks watching each other; their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do."

The plaintiffs are represented by Bathaee Dunne LLP. Samsung is represented by O'Melveny & Myers LLP, SK Hynix by Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP, and Micron by Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP.

Judge Wise ordered the companies to answer by Dec. 7, 2026. Because the court had reset argument by about three weeks, she also granted the companies' unopposed administrative motion to continue early case deadlines and reset the initial case management conference for Jan. 12, 2027, at 9 a.m.
